subject: Private endpoint IP ownership, allowlist and firewall policy
messages:
From: Liam Carter <liam.carter@edgewave.com>
To: Sofia Ivanova <sofia.ivanova@redwood.ai>
Cc: security_ops@edgewave.com
Date: Mon, 02 Feb 2026 09:13:00 -0800
Subject: Private endpoint allowlist + egress questions

Hi Sofia,

Thanks again for the walkthrough this morning. A couple of follow-ups from our security team as we prepare the VPC peering and firewall changes:

- We need a canonical list of outbound IPs (and whether they are stable) to add to our perimeter allowlist.
- Clarify if Redwood's private endpoint requires any inbound ports open on our side beyond standard HTTPS (443).
- Confirm whether you expect any egress to external services (license checks, telemetry) from the private control plane and the ranges for those.

Can you also attach any diagrams of how your control plane communicates with customer VPCs so we can map to our firewall vendor rules?

Best,
Liam
Liam Carter
Senior InfoSec Engineer
EdgeWave Systems
From: Sofia Ivanova <sofia.ivanova@redwood.ai>
To: Liam Carter <liam.carter@edgewave.com>
Cc: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>, Connor O'Brien <connor.obrien@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 02 Feb 2026 10:01:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Private endpoint allowlist + egress questions

Thanks Liam — short answers up front, details/attachments below.

1) Outbound IPs: we publish a small, rotating set of egress IPs per-region for the control plane and a separate set for the data-plane (model inference). The control-plane list is intended to be stable across quarters; data-plane ranges may change with capacity scaling but we provide CIDR ranges and a two-week notice when changes occur. I've attached the current CSV with both lists.

2) Inbound ports: customer VPCs must allow outbound HTTPS (443) to our private endpoint IPs — we do NOT require any inbound ports into the customer's VPC. All communication is initiated from the VPC to Redwood.

3) Egress to external services: the control plane will make occasional HTTPS calls to our telemetry and license services; these originate from the control-plane IP set. For model serving (data plane) there is no mandatory external egress unless you enable optional integrations (metrics exporters, S3 backends) — those are documented and toggled per-deployment.

Attachments included: redwood-private-endpoint-ip-list.csv, egress-policy-diagram.png, ma-planned-firewall-rules.md

Below is a brief mapping and recommended firewall entries you can paste to your vendor:

-- Recommended rules (customer outbound) --
- Allow TCP 443 to 34.198.10.0/24 (control-plane US-west)
- Allow TCP 443 to 52.210.200.0/22 (data-plane US-west, inference)
- Allow TCP 443 to 35.100.50.128/25 (control-plane telemetry)

Notes:
- Our control-plane uses TLS mutual auth for management APIs; we expect TLS termination on our side only.
- If you operate strict egress inspection (TLS MITM), that will break mTLS and is not supported for control-plane endpoints — recommend bypass for the listed IPs.

I'll loop Rishi/Connor for technical verification and any additional constraints.

Thanks,
Sofia Ivanova
Head of Solutions (Private Deploy)
Redwood Inference
From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>
To: Sofia Ivanova <sofia.ivanova@redwood.ai>, Liam Carter <liam.carter@edgewave.com>
Cc: Connor O'Brien <connor.obrien@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 02 Feb 2026 11:24:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Private endpoint allowlist + egress questions

Liam / Sofia — quick technical clarifications:

- CIDR granularity: the CSV groups ranges by /24 (control) and /22 (data-plane). If your vendor needs single IPs, we can provide a pinned list for an additional commitment window (we do that for dedicated customers).
- NAT vs. SNAT: for on-prem private deployments behind a NAT gateway, ensure the NAT preserves source IP mapping if you intend to do any on-prem access controls; otherwise treat egress as coming from the NAT IPs you will list.
- TLS interception: as Sofia mentioned, we use mTLS on the control plane. If your egress proxy performs TLS interception, we need an exception for the control-plane CIDRs to avoid breaking enrollment and webhook callbacks.
- DNS: do not rely on hostnames alone for allowlisting; we sign our certificate names but provide IP ranges as the authoritative routing filter.

Connor, can you confirm whether our control-plane publishes a weekly checksum file of the CSV so customers can automate detection of changes?

-Rishi
Director, Platform Security
Redwood Inference
From: Connor O'Brien <connor.obrien@redwood.ai>
To: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>, Sofia Ivanova <sofia.ivanova@redwood.ai>, Liam Carter <liam.carter@edgewave.com>
Date: Mon, 02 Feb 2026 16:37:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Private endpoint allowlist + egress questions

Confirming: yes, we publish a signed manifest (SHA256) for the CSV on the same drive link. We also publish a weekly changelog and a two-week deprecation notice for any range removal. For customers who need static IPs we offer a pinned IP addendum under Dedicated contracts — we can scope that if EdgeWave is interested.

I also want to call out one operational recommendation for your firewall rules: keep an allowlist for both the control-plane *and* a separate one for data-plane bursts. This prevents accidental mixing of model traffic with management traffic and makes troubleshooting simpler.

Connor O'Brien
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference
